name: Chinese (Simplified)
signature: Each character is a dense, evenly-sized square block of strokes — not an alphabet of letters at all.
combination: Not an alphabet: each CHARACTER (hànzì) writes a whole syllable/morpheme, and words are one or more characters (你好 = 'you' + 'good' = hello). Characters are built from recurring COMPONENTS called radicals — often one hinting at meaning and one at sound (a phono-semantic compound: 请 qǐng = 讠 'speech' + 青 qīng 'sound'). Stroke order is a real, taught system (top→bottom, left→right, horizontal before vertical, outside before inside), so — unlike the Indic scripts here — the strokeOrder below is authoritative, not merely conventional.
notes: Simplified characters. The inventory closes the current Mandarin lesson corpus with greeting/self-introduction characters, numerals one to five, and the radicals they decompose into; it must grow whenever the track adds vocabulary. `sound` is tone-marked pinyin; `tone` holds the number (1–4 or neutral) and indexes into `tones` below. The font is a fonttools subset of NotoSansSC covering exactly these characters (see _fonts/README.md); re-subset when characters are added.

tones.name: first (high level)
tones.description: Held high and flat, like humming one steady note. English has no equivalent: the pitch does not rise or fall at all.

tones.name: second (rising)
tones.description: Rises from mid to high, the way an English speaker's pitch rises on a surprised "huh?".

tones.name: third (dipping / low)
tones.description: Dips low and creaky, then rises a little if the syllable is said alone. In running speech it usually stays low and never climbs back up.

tones.name: fourth (falling)
tones.description: Drops sharply from high to low, like a clipped English "No!".

tones.name: neutral (unstressed)
tones.description: Short, light, and pitched by whatever came before it. Written with no mark at all.

toneSandhi.description: When two third tones meet, the first is said as a second (rising) tone. The spelling and the dictionary pinyin never change, so the written form and the spoken form differ on purpose.
不 bù drops to bú before a fourth-tone syllable.

letters.notes: Means 'four'. Breaks the stroke-count pattern of 一二三: four stacked bars would be unreadable, so 四 is a borrowed shape.
